utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Registrar, please call the case. I didn't call you Madam this morning, so that should please you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a chair. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness I understand is very anxious to return back home. So Mr. Ackerman -- are there any preliminaries before? Okay, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just need to remind you that you are still -- the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth still holds good today. So remember that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Witness needs to be given DB172 through DB180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. DB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, I think you have DB172 in front of you now. And this is -- this series of documents are the documents that you brought with you. Could you please just explain to the Chamber what DB172 is.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, 172, was written on the 1st of December 1992 by the minister of construction and signed by Minister Brdjanin. In this letter addressed to the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska and relates to the protection of buildings and facilities in the territory of Republika Srpska. We read that it has been noticed in areas where combat is still taking place between the warring parties. When a certain part of the territory is liberated, civilians tend to devastate facilities that had not been destroyed by the war, taking away building materials and other things, other property. The minister requires from these two authorities, the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff, to protect these facilities to establish commissions in order to confiscate such material, store it, and put it under the protection of civilian authorities to be used later for accommodation of refugees coming from other regions. This letter also suggests that these cases should be sanctioned and held under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of your own knowledge whether this letter actually had any impact or effect?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my own experience I know that this letter had a great impact. However, it arrived a little too late because a lot of these facilities had been destroyed before this letter reached the ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look now at DB173. This appears to be another letter issued by Mr. Brdjanin on 28 December 1992. Could you simply explain this letter to the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The director of a big Banja Luka enterprise is addressing the ministry, and Minister Brdjanin personally asking for help in providing housing for the employees of that enterprise. Mr. Brdjanin writes this letter to this big company called Incel, personally addressed to the director, saying that this is a republic with a rule of law where regardless of the war, nobody has the right to administer their own justice at gunpoint and at their own consideration, and to jeopardise public property, thinking that it is enough to put on a uniform of Republika Srpska to have such rights. He also mentions that soldiers and the families of soldiers who were killed do have a right to housing, but not to acquiring it by force or by evicting somebody else. That is the gist of the letter. And at the end, there is a sentence that says: "If such incidents occur again in the future, you should inform the army command of the Army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now have you look at DB174. And this document is dated 12 August 1994.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This ministry and Mr. Brdjanin write a letter to the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka; that is, the MUP, addressed personally to the chief. And the subject is "eviction of squatters or illegal tenants." There were a lot of squatters, and they needed to be evicted. If civilians needed to be evicted, it was not a big problem because the municipality had adopted a determination on evictions. And the police would assist in this procedure, and the squatter would be evicted easily. However, in cases where the squatters were members of the police, the municipality would institute proceedings to evict them; but in those cases, the police force would not come to assist in the eviction of illegal tenants who were at the same time members of the police. The minister, therefore, is writing this letter to the chief of the Security Services Centre saying that there had been a lot of such cases, a lot of reports had been filed involving members of the police, even instructors in the police academy. And the minister insists that regardless of who an eviction involves, legal provisions need to be observed and enforced. That is the gist of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it refers specifically to one employee by the name of Zeljko Skrbic, a former member of the MUP special unit now employed at the school of internal affairs who is illegally occupying a flat and needs to be evicted. Correct? In the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look please at DB175 now, then.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we see here is an enactment wherein the ministry circulates a letter to all administrative boards of municipalities concerning the rationalisation of housing stock. Namely, in end 1993 the people's assembly enacted a law on the rationalisation of housing stock which implies that every person who is occupying a large apartment without really needing so much space should be moved to a more appropriately sized apartment so as to make room for large families or families of refugees who do need housing. However, in reality, it was noticed that this law was not being implemented in all municipalities properly, so the Minister Brdjanin circulated this letter to all municipalities saying that socially owned apartments should be rationalised strictly in keeping with the law, moving into apartments only people who have appropriate decisions or determinations allowing them to do so, insisting also that nobody should be left out in the street, and that the law should be enforced equally regardless of who is involved. I know that many such letters have been addressed to Executive Boards of municipalities. In fact, every time when it was noted that illegal actions are taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next document is DB176.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter is phrased similarly. And the intent behind it is the same. The only difference is that it is addressed to a large electrical Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. company in Banja Luka, and it was motivated by complaints by individual citizens who came to complain to the ministry. And then the ministry wrote this letter with the same message that is contained in the law, insisting that the law must be enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next one is DB177.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an approval for exchange of apartments. As I told you in my earlier testimony, I described the procedure for giving approval for apartment exchange, housing exchange. We see here that this particular flat was owned by republican authorities. In such cases, the occupant had to address republican authorities asking for their approval. In this case, it was Irfan Nurudinovic an ethnic Muslim who asked for this approval wishing to exchange apartments with Jovanka Sobic. The Minister hereby gives this approval. Everything is strictly in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is a Muslim resident of Banja Luka in March of 1993 wanting to exchange with -- is it a Serb resident of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by the name, it is a Serb lady. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go then to Document 178.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, we see another approval for exchange of real estate. The applicant is a Croat, Joso Pranjic from Banja Luka who wishes to swap flats with Mladen Koljancic from Sisak. And in this case, the ministry established that the intent behind this application is to move out and move into a different apartment, and the change of residence, change of the place of residence. Therefore, the ministry gave its approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next one is DB179. This one is 20 October 1994. This appears that someone actually came to the minister to complain about his situation.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. From this document, we see that somebody came to complain to the ministry. In this case, it was Vjekoslav Psorn, a person of Croat ethnicity. He emphasises here that he has a contract and an apartment, and that nevertheless his company allocated his apartment to another employee, moving him to a smaller apartment. Since the ministry judged that the law was violated here, it instructed the company to implement the legal procedure and to reconsider again whether the person in question should be indeed moved to a smaller apartment or not. We are talking about the Rotas company of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what is the ethnicity of Vjekoslav?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it already. It's Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go to DB180, the final document in this group.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a peculiar case. I am personally familiar with this, as is almost everyone employed at our ministry. The family involved is very prominent in Banja Luka. Krsto Schubert, I believe, is of foreign provenance, Austrian or something. And his wife is from Banja Luka, a Muslim. And in this case, they were subjected to a decision on rationalisation; that is, moved to a smaller apartment. This family complained to the ministry, and the minister, Brdjanin, wrote a letter to the municipality instructing them to suspend eviction proceedings regarding the Schubert family until their complaint is reviewed by a higher Court. I know that this family was not evicted at the time, and I'm not sure whether they continued to live in that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We're finished, then, with those documents. I want to know if you know an individual from Celinac by the name of -- I think the name is Irfan Tatilic or something like that, a school director.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Irfan very well. His last name is Tetaric. He's a director of a school, a very prominent citizen of Celinac, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the period when Mr. Brdjanin was president of the Executive Board in Celinac, was he able to maintain his position with that school?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't know. Mr. Tetaric was director of that school for a long time. He was getting on, soon to be retired. I know that he lived in Celinac all that time. He was a very cooperative citizen. His daughter was a lawyer and worked for the municipal authorities under me. She worked there, and I know her father lived in Celinac at the time, and I know that she left Celinac for Zenica just before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to look now at one more document. It is Document P2330, 2-3-3-0. You've seen this document before a day or two ago. And in your capacity as a lawyer and as someone who has been active in various ministries for a number of years, I want to ask you to take a look at Article 46 of this document, the law on internal affairs, and give the Chamber your interpretation of the meaning of Article 46.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been a lawyer for a long time. I helped write a lot of laws, but in the area of town planning, environmental protection, and construction, my field of expertise. This text that I'm reading is difficult to interpret for any lawyer unless you know the entire text of this law. I am not familiar with the entirety of this law, but this article, 46, as I understand it, says that in discharging duties and responsibilities related to the protection of constitutional order, human lives, and the personal safety of citizens or security of citizens, the minister or any other authorised official or, in special cases, other officials authorised by the minister may issue special orders to citizens, companies, and other legal entities. This is an authorisation of the minister or another authorised official, assistant minister or deputy minister or perhaps a lower ranking civil servant authorised by the minister to issue such orders. If this is the law on internal affairs, it must be referring to senior officials within the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When it refers to the other authorised officials, that means officials within the Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understand it. This law applies to internal affairs, so that must be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A few days ago the question arose as to whether -- the last two words of that article, legal entities, has any specific meaning. Can you tell us if it does; and if so, what does "legal entities" mean, what does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This moment, I can't say anything because this last sentence can refer to something else. I would have to be familiar with the integral text of this law which is rather long. Then I would be able to see whether these authorities may be transferred to somebody else. However, bearing in mind how laws were drafted in the former Yugoslavia, at least to my knowledge, this article, to my mind, should have concerned the relationships and command authority within the Ministry itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think -- let me try to make that question a little more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we are there, and I don't think you are going to get there, Mr. Ackerman. I would leave the question to someone who is more competent on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's probably fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are free to continue, to proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- But I don't think you are going to get where you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I may try one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we just look at this law as the Minister being able in emergency situations to issue orders to certain entities, it says to citizens, companies, and other legal entities, the question we have -- and if you don't know it, it's fine, just say you don't know - but the question we have is what kind of organisations would be contemplated by the term "other legal entities"? For instance, could that be a municipal Crisis Staff or not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, when I asked you - it's in page 8, line 17 - I asked you -- you were talking about the daughter of this gentleman, Irfan. The transcript indicates that you said that she left Celinac before the war, and I'm told that what you said was that she left at the end of the war and went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember what I said. However, I know this woman very well. I was her superior. She worked in the electoral committee of the first multiparty elections. Later on, she was in charge of issuing work permits and work licenses. I saw her in 1994. I remember it only too well when she was still discharging these duties. I also heard, and I know that towards the end of the war, she left Celinac. She went to Zenica, and she works in the Municipal Assembly of Zenica. I can't remember the date when she departed, but I remember that in 1994 she still worked with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That clears that up, and that's all the questions I have for you, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're now going to be cross-examined by Ms. Ann Sutherland for the Prosecution. I need to draw your attention to a basic rule here, basic rule of procedure, and also of fairness and natural justice, and that is that as a witness here, even though you have been brought over by the Defence as a Defence witness, you are basically a witness for truth and justice. So your duty under the oath that you took yesterday is to answer all questions truthfully and fully, irrespective of who is putting those questions to you. So your duty extends also to all the questions that Ms. Sutherland will be putting to you. If there are any questions that you feel you ought not to answer, then draw my attention, and it will be myself and the two Judges flanking me that will decide whether you ought to answer the question or not. Otherwise, your duty is to answer all questions. I recognise Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I neglected to offer and tender Exhibits DB154 through DB159; DB166 through DB169; DB170 through DB180.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they are also being admitted. Thank you. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you said yesterday at page 47 of the LiveNote that you worked as a technical secretary of the Celinac Municipality, and you worked as a secretary of the executive committee until November 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were appointed by the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you want me, I can clarify. In the legal system before the multiparty elections, there was a position of the secretary of the Executive Board. I discharged those duties between 1983 and 1984. However, after the multiparty elections, new rules were drafted, and there was no longer the secretary of the Executive Board as a position because a new position was established. And that was the chief of service for joint affairs who was also discharging the duties of the former secretary of the Executive Board. So I was issued a decision to be appointed chief of services -- of joint and common services. And in that position, I also executed the duties of the technical secretary of the Executive Board. I don't know whether you have understood me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still don't have a clear-cut answer as to who appointed you actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who signed the decision?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was signed by the president of the Executive Board. That was my appointment to the position of the chief of joint services which discharged all the technical and administrative duties for the Executive Boards because according to this new law, there was no longer position of the secretary of the Executive Board as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, I would ask if you could keep your answers short. So in other words, if I understood you, you worked for both the Municipal Assembly and the executive committee or Executive Board? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Municipal Assembly is a higher body. I didn't work for the Municipal Assembly. I only worked for the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you didn't attend the Municipal Assembly sessions, and you weren't responsible for technically preparing those sessions?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Another person did that. The secretary of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said yesterday that you were responsible for getting together all of the decisions relating to things that were discussed by the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that. And this is the truth. The Executive Committee discusses one set of things, and the Municipal Assembly as a higher body discusses another set of things. The secretary of the Municipal Assembly was involved in the preparation of their sessions, and it was not me. For the Executive Board, I was the one who was performing all such duties for the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was the secretary to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the Municipal Assembly after the multiparty elections was Dusko Djajic and later on Andjelko Topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you were unable to present and someone else stood in your position, in order to carry out your job properly, did you read transcripts of proceedings and decisions which had been arrived at?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What minutes are you referring to? Are you referring to the minutes of the Executive Committee or the minutes of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can -- anyway, I don't understand -- I don't understand why you're mixing it up with the Municipal Assembly now once you've just confirmed to us that you had nothing to do with the Municipal Assembly. So there was no reason why you could have misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood the question. Madam Prosecutor asked me questions about both the assembly and the Executive Committee. So to answer this question, I was not in the position to read the transcripts of the Municipal Assembly. The Municipal Assembly is a higher body, and I didn't have to do that. As for the Executive Committee transcripts, I had to read those because I myself did not take the minutes. It was somebody else who was in charge of taking the minutes of these sessions, and I had to read them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The minute taker for the Executive Board or the Executive Committee, was that a person by the name of Vujatovic?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Marica Vujatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you answer my question, please. Was that person the minute taker for the Executive Committee or the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. It was not always the same person who took the minutes. But very often, it was Marica Vujatovic or Rada Djombic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You discussed yesterday at page 48 and following for the Court the difference between a decision and a conclusion. And you agreed with Mr. Ackerman's question that a conclusion was more of an advisory nature than that of a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown DB164, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is an Official Gazette published in March 1992. If you could look, please, at the law on government. And if I can take you to part 6, "regulations and other enactments of the government," Article 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem? What was the problem? We all seem to have it, no? You don't have it in B/C/S? I can't help you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have a B/C/S version. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I took it from something that the witness said yesterday he also understands English, no?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Do you want to check that it is the same document, Mr. Ackerman, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm satisfied it's the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would it be possible for the interpreters to get a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of which version, the English or the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Both would be nice if available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, you can give the -- is this going to be a long question or the beginning of a series of questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There's a couple of questions, Your Honour, so I think it would be helpful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so usher, you can give the interpreters my copy, and then bring it back to me, please. But I don't have the original -- the version in the original language. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, Article 20 says that the government shall issue decrees, decisions, instructions, resolutions, and conclusions, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can take you to Article 20 of the law on government which is on page number -- the ERN at the bottom of the page, 00184299.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually understand your question. However, you asked me how was it that I said that the Executive Committee issued conclusions. And here in front of me, I see Article 20 of the law on the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it's -- however, the duties of the Executive Committee are regulated by an enactment of the Executive Board rather than by the law on government of Republika Srpska. Here it says that these are the enactments which may be passed by the government. At that time, I didn't work in the government, and I believe that I cannot answer your question for that fact. The duties of an Executive Committee are regulated by a different enactment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you wait for my question, you will see whether you can answer it. My question to you was: Under Article 20, it says there that the government has issue decrees, decisions, instructions, resolutions, and conclusions, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that article say what Ms. Sutherland is suggesting to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I can read it for you. "In the discharge of its rights and duties as established in the constitution and law, the government shall issue decrees, decisions, instructions, resolutions, and conclusions." Do you see that paragraph, the first paragraph under Article 20?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have it. In my copy, it says in the exercise, it is constitutionally provided for duties, the government issues decrees, instructions, decisions, and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. You just said that duties of the Executive Committee are regulated by an enactment of the Executive Board, rather than this law on government. But my question to you is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I don't know the language. But I can count at least. This is the first paragraph of Article 20, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I am starting from the last word in the second line of the first paragraph of Article 20, and that last word before the comma should be "decrees". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So if that is correct, after there are one, two, three, and four. So it's five. What you read initially would count to five: Has issued decrees, decisions, instructions, resolutions, and conclusions. The witness is leaving resolutions out. He's saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you could ask the witness to read slowly, we will interpret again. It was too fast for the interpreters to get the entire sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please read the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Ackerman is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, give them the B/C/S version. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I saw you standing, but I hadn't finished as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I fear that we're getting into mass confusion here. You'll recall that when Mr. Treanor was testifying, he talked about the organisation of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. What we're looking at here is the law on government which Mr. Treanor described as what previously would have been the Executive Body, or the Executive Committee. It's headed by a prime minister, two deputy prime minister, and all of these other ministers. So this refers to the operation of that organisation only. It has nothing to do with municipal boards, Executive Boards, anything like that. So we're mixing apples and oranges here, and as long as everybody understands that's what we're doing that's okay. But I think there's confusion about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I preferred to keep silent because I don't know what the question is. The question could well be to distinguish between all these decrees, et cetera, and that would be very relevant and that's why I didn't try to jump the gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I understand the difference very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please read the first paragraph under Article 20, and can you read it slowly for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Sometimes, sir, you have to be patient with us because here the process is that what you're saying is -- has to be translated into English and into French. What I am saying has to be translated into French and your own language. And it goes on and on, so one has to speak slowly, and usually I am the first one to commit the mistake, to make the mistake. So go ahead and read out the first paragraph of Article 20, please, as slowly as you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In exercising its rights and duties as stipulated by the constitution and the law, the government shall adopted decrees, decisions, instructions, resolutions, and conclusions." This is exactly what the Presiding Judge said a little while ago. You said that I didn't mention "resolutions." A resolution in B/C/S is not a resolution. It is an administrative enactment which is adopted by an administrative body, and this is exactly what it says here. So "resolution" for our purposes should be "determination."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, then it goes on to spell out what decrees shall regulate, decisions shall regulate, instructions shall prescribe, and the government shall issue resolutions in certain matters. And then it goes on to say: "In its conclusions, the government shall establish its position on matters which are not regulated by decrees, decisions, and instructions, and establish the obligations of government working bodies as well as the preparation of materials for the government and the national assembly." Do you see that there in the final paragraph? Yes or no. Do you see what I have just read to you about conclusions in the final paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. It is in the last paragraph of this article.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So nowhere in Article 20 does it say that a conclusion is less obligatory than decrees, decisions, instructions, or resolutions, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. It's not relevant to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. testimony he was giving. He was talking about pronouncements of Executive Board, Crisis Staff, things like that, not the government of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To it's apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not. One can draw inferences, Mr. Ackerman. So the question is perfectly legitimate. Answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did talk about the conclusions of the government, conclusions adopted by the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pause there, sir. My question to you was nowhere in Article 20 does it say that a conclusion is less obligatory than decrees, decisions, instructions, or resolutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's stick to Article 20 for the time being. Do you agree with Ms. Sutherland is suggesting to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my understanding, it was always the case that a conclusion is a milder enactment than those that the lady enumerated before it. And it just provided for certain activities, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question is that Article 20 does not really make this distinction as to the weight that each one of these provisions taken would carry. There's no distinction made between them in Article 20. That is what is being suggested to you. Do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are indeed great differences. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show me where in Article 20 you see these differences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see differences in the description of what is governed by a decree as opposed to what is governed by a decision and what is specified and stipulated by instructions, whereas conclusions are adopted by the government on issues that are not stipulated. That is, other issues that have not been covered by the previous types of enactments. In other words, the government, through its conclusions, simply adopts a certain stand on something, a position. What is not regulated by instructions or decisions as legal enactments is reflected in conclusions wherein the government takes a certain position on an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. He's your witness, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, one last question on this: In fact, the law refers to obligations which may be imposed by a conclusion, does it not? That's what the last paragraph in Article 20 says; it's referring to obligations. The word is "obveza."

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But in the form of regulating standards, and we lawyers understand what regulating standard means as applied to the implementation of certain activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Could the witness be shown P80. Then for the Court Deputy's benefit, then I would like to show the Witness P227, and then P258.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't recall getting a list of the exhibits that they were going to use in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Gustin is having it printed out as we speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hope I can get an apology for all the times I was berated for not doing what they have just not done.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is not in a position to determine what documents they are going to use in cross-examination until they have heard the whole of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can I take you to the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina dated September 1991. Can I take you to Article 35. And that is under part V, acts of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. In particular, the second paragraph: "Decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of the municipalities." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. And to this question, I can answer that I'm seeing this statute for the first time, and I'm seeing it for the first time because I never worked as secretary of the assembly, and I never had any contact with the autonomous region. But if you allow me to voice the opinion I have based on what I heard and what I learned here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you because the question was whether you're seeing that article. For the time being, just answer whether you have it in front of you or not. Read it, and then the next question will follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 35: "Prior to the adoption of decisions, conclusions, and stands on issues of vital importance for the performance of the determined or stipulated functions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, if so requested by at least ten members of the assembly, opinions shall be obtained from member municipalities. Decisions and conclusions of the assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the members of municipalities." I did understand this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've just read for the Court Article 35. Can I take you to Article 38. That's under part VII, and it talks about amendments to the statute. I don't want to you read the entire paragraph. Can you just read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in there, it talks about if any proposal to amend the statute should be communicated to the assemblies of the member municipalities for consideration in order to obtain their opinions.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want you to now look at Exhibit P227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's the big Official Gazette number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We must give the usher time to find the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was simply telling him it was a big document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, okay. Doesn't seem that big to me. Is this what you wanted, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, that is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina issue number 2, published in Banja Luka on the 5th of June 1992. And it contains 28 decisions and conclusions and decrees. Could I take you to decision numbered 17, and that is a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For you, that appears on the page that has the number at the top 00497849. Do you see the number at the top?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you can go down towards the bottom of the page, it's decision numbered 17. And it's "conclusions reached at the Crisis Staff meeting of the ARK held on the 26th of May 1992." And I take you to paragraph 1: "The work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has absolute support since it is now the highest organ of authority in the Autonomous Region of Krajina as the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina cannot function due to objective and subjective circumstances." The following paragraph: "Decisions of Crisis Staffs are binding for all Crisis Staffs in the municipalities." And the third paragraph: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "These decisions of the Crisis Staff shall be submitted for verification to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina as soon as it is able to convene." Do you see those three paragraphs, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I take you now to Exhibit P258. Exhibit P258 is the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina number 3 of 1992, published in Banja Luka on the 23rd of June 1992. And it contains decisions numbered 29 to 47, decisions and decrees and conclusions. Can you look, please, at decision number 42, which appears on the page numbered at the bottom of the page 00389000. And that decision: "The Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina at its meeting held on the 15th of June 1992 took the following decision on amending and supplementing the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" which is the document that you saw just a moment ago. Article 1 of that decision states that paragraph 2 of the Article 35 of the Statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina is hereby amended to read: "The decisions and conclusions of the Assembly must be respected by the municipalities." And Article 2 states when the decision shall enter into force. Do you see that decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you still have P80, the Autonomous Region of Krajina statute in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You may recall, and I will read it for you, that paragraph 2 of the Article 35 to which this decision of the 15th of June 1992 refers, it states that decisions and conclusions of the assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the member municipalities." And now, that is amended to read: "The decisions and conclusions of the assembly must be respected by the municipalities." So, sir, decisions and conclusions, here, of the same weight. Are they not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say much about these documents, and I cannot give you full answers because first of all I see them for the first time. Second, I did not work on their wording myself. I didn't work with the Crisis Staff of the municipality or the Crisis Staff of the region or the autonomous region itself. I can only speak on the basis of how I understand this at first glance. This question had better be asked of the people who really worked on the drafting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But do you agree that on the face of the documents that I have shown you, where the ARK Crisis Staff on the 26th of May 1992 says they are the highest organ in the region, and that all decisions are binding on municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- And conclusions. And then some two weeks to three weeks later, a decision amending the statute to say that decisions and conclusions must be respected by the municipalities taking away the previous paragraph, saying that they were only binding after the Municipal Assemblies passed them. Do you agree that on the face of these documents, that is correct, and that there's no distinction between decisions and conclusions?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to let me say a few words because I managed to put things together in my head. In Article 35 of the statute, it says, as far as I understand it, that when somebody submits a motion to the assembly for consideration, the assembly has first to canvass the joint municipalities for their opinions. After that is done, and after the assembly makes a decision, that decision, judging by paragraph 2 of Article -- of this article, is only applicable after being approved by the assemblies of municipalities, or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It says -- paragraph 1 of Article 35 says: "The Autonomous Region of Krajina shall, if so requested by at least ten members of the Assembly, obtain the opinions..."

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If they are requested, it's not mandatory that they do so. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, it's not mandatory. But it applies if verified by the assemblies of joint municipalities. But the other two issues are related to this issue. And the other two provisions are a bit different because on one hand, we see pristine problems and issues, whereas on the other hand we have a situation of the state of war or the immediate threat of war where the Crisis Staff replaces civilian authorities until further notice, until a time when they're able to convene again. And it is defined in this way here. I am not fully conversant with this issue, but there must have been situations in reality that motivated this particular phrasing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try to draw this part of the testimony to an end at least. Going back to all the documents that you have been shown by Ms. Sutherland on this question of conclusions, decisions, instructions, resolutions, and whatever, did you see any document where the conclusion is or would be that conclusions are not binding, while decisions, for example, are always binding? Did you see anywhere being stated that conclusions are not binding? Or is the general refrain always that irrespective of the terminology used and the name given, they are always decisions and they are always binding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From my experience, I know that when I'm writing conclusions and applying them, what I said applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not referring to your experience. I am referring to your eyes. Did you see anywhere in these documents words to the effect that conclusions reached by whoever are not binding while other decisions are binding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. This conclusion number 17, which I talked about, provides absolute support, accepts a report. That is the terminology of issues governed by conclusions under our system. This decision amending the statute was adopted by the Crisis Staff. And in Article 2, it says that quite understandably, it will be verified by the assembly of the autonomous region when all the conditions for that are met, when it becomes possible for them to meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, just before we have a break and go on to another topic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, just before we have a break and go on to another topic, I just want to go back to what we discussed first this morning. Do I understand that you were head of the joint technical service in the Celinac municipality of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Nothing to do with the Municipal Assembly, and she just asked him if he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Technical service in the Celinac -- Municipal Assembly. He had nothing to do with the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's the Municipal Assembly, and this is the joint technical service in the Celinac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought the witness answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question contains the words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't change anything, Mr. Ackerman. He's not being asked whether he formed part of the Municipal Assembly. He's being asked whether he was the head of the joint technical service in the Celinac Municipality. Were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is true that I was the head of service for joint affairs which dealt with all the joint affairs of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Executive Board, the Municipal Assembly, and all the municipal authorities. That is what the organisational scheme was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it was answerable to whom, to which body, the joint --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was accountable to the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as head of the joint technical services department, did you attend the Municipal Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is the secretary of the Municipal Assembly who attended them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is a convenient -- it's 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it you haven't finished your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was just hopeful. 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, a moment ago you said that you were head of the joint technical services department which dealt with all the affairs of the Executive Board, the Municipal Assembly, and all the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're aware that a Crisis Staff was formed in the Celinac Municipality, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said on page 51 of your testimony yesterday: "I never worked in the war presidency, and I have absolutely no information about their dealings." Do you still maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, I was not a member. I did not discharge any significant duties for them. I may have done some marginal things, but I don't remember that I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What would you call marginal?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During a certain period of time, the Municipal Assembly could not be convened. And the Crisis Staff replaced that body. Maybe, the joint affairs department at that time were asked to be of service, of technical service to that body, maybe to do the transcript or other such things. But that is all I can remember. But it would have been an obligation of joint affairs department in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "maybe to do the transcript," you're talking about the recording of the Crisis Staff sessions?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Taking minutes of all the bodies that worked at that time, including the Crisis Staff. There was probably not a designated person to take minutes there. It would always be somebody else who took minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall now the names of any of the people who may have taken the minutes at the Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been recording secretaries who usually did it at regular sessions. It could have also been the secretary of the assembly. It could have also been everybody who was an official in the municipal body and who was given the task to take the minutes on any given day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned, I think, Andjelko Topic as being the secretary of the Municipal Assembly. Is that who you are referring to when you said a moment ago the secretary of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could have been Andjelko Topic or anybody else tasked by the president of the Crisis Staff to take the minutes. This is nothing special. A person who is a recording secretary for a particular session just makes notes of what is said during discussions. That person is not in charge of drafting any conclusions or drafting any decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where would those minutes, the transcripts of the recordings, be? Where would they be filed? Where would they be kept?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Most probably they're kept by the secretary of the Municipal Assembly or the president of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff replaced the service of the technical secretary of the Municipal Assembly and the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So what normally happens to the transcripts and the recordings of the sessions of the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board? Where are they filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have a question. When Ms. Sutherland refers to "recordings and transcript," I wonder if she means audiorecordings and transcripts made there from and if the witness understands that that's what she understands or if she has a different understanding of what she means by recordings and transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a fair question. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned recordings earlier. The person who is a recording secretary for a particular session makes notes. I'm referring to those recorded notes, whether they be in audio form or written form.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, they were only kept in written form. And I believe that this is the case even to this very day, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As head of the joint technical services department in charge of the technical aspects of the assembly and the Executive Board, you would be in a position to know where these things are filed, when the assembly and the Executive Board was running prewar. Where are they filed normally?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it very well. When it comes to the Executive Board, all enactments passed by the Executive Boards are kept in the file with the secretary of the Executive Board or in the files of the Executive Board. And as for the files of the Municipal Assembly, they are kept by the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, some of it is kept by the president, and in the service which is a special service consisting of two clerks working for the assembly. So these are two separate sets of files, absolutely separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I am perhaps not being clear enough. I'm talking about where are they physically filed? Where would they be? In whose filing cabinet, in whose offices?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be in the office of the secretary of the assembly. While I was discharging those duties, they were kept in my filing cabinet. After that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where are the archives situated?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The joint archives for all the organs used to be in one place. And particular cases which have not been filed in permanent documentation, I've told you where they are. They're kept either one or the other secretary, the respective secretaries of the Executive Board or the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that answer your question, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where was the joint archive for all the organs?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically, it was located on the ground floor, and the -- it was all registered and there was a person in charge of looking after all these files in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We've seen you brought some documents from the Ministry with you, be Exhibits DB170 through DB180. Were you asked to bring any documents from the Celinac Crisis Staff meetings with you or any documents pertaining to the Celinac Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked me to do that. There's no way for me to get hold of any documents of the Crisis Staff. And I don't want to have anything Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to do with any of the Crisis Staff, either of the Krajina staff or the Celinac staff. I don't know who has custody of all that documentation. I don't know much about this documentation or any of the decisions that were passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why don't you want to have anything to do with any of the Crisis Staff, either of the Krajina staff or the Celinac staff?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be very honest here, although I'm in the public eye. I didn't ask for the war. I didn't want the war to happen. I wanted to be as far away as possible from the war and from all the Crisis Staffs. Nobody ever asked me to join them, and even if they had asked me, I would have tried to get away from that somehow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you look at Exhibit P1993. Sir, have you finished reading that document?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of it. I have read item 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, that's a decision of the Municipal Assembly of Celinac at its session held on the 13th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Appointing persons to the Crisis Staff of the Celinac Municipality. And we can see under paragraph 1, Sveto Kovacevic is appointed as president; number 2, Radoslav Brdjanin as a member.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then another nine members. Had you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I take you to paragraph 3. It says the Crisis Staff shall coordinate the functions of authority, and through coordination, the Crisis Staff will create conditions for the municipal Executive Committee to exercise its legal exact power and govern the economy and other aspects of life. Is it really your position today that you've never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my position that I never saw this document before. I don't remember all of these people. I remember some of the people who were members of the Crisis Staff, but if you had asked me earlier to give you all of their names, I wouldn't have been able to do that. Since the assembly could not be convened, the Executive Committee worked regularly and had a number of sessions. I don't know how many, and I don't know what tasks it had at the time. But one of its tasks was to organise the economy and all the social activities under the given circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And therefore, from what you've just said, you must have realised that the Municipal Assembly wasn't convening and that you, as head of the joint technical service, now came under the Crisis Staff of the Celinac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the assembly could not be convened, and the Crisis Staff is the body that organises life in the municipality, replacing the municipality, and all the duties were discharged by the secretary of the assembly which wasn't me. And my employees, my typists, my drivers, or possibly some other members of staff were obliged to carry out tasks given to them by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were aware Mr. Brdjanin was a member, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he was a member or not, I can see in this decision that he was. If you had asked me before that whether he was a member, I wouldn't have been able to tell you whether he was or not. I don't know how many meetings they had, what things they discussed at those meetings, who attended these meetings, whether Mr. Brdjanin attended those meetings once, several times or not at all. I am really not in a position to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you held this position until November 1990 -- 1992, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff would have been meeting in the same building where you were working.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have to mean that. I don't know how meetings were called, where they were held. I suppose that those meetings were held in the same places where the sessions of the Municipal Assembly are held, or the services that existed even before that. There was no reason whatsoever to hold meetings anywhere else. This was just one body replacing the Municipal Assembly at that given moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff were meeting in the municipal building, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure that they were. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And your offices were in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as head of the joint technical service of the Executive Committee, you would have had dealings with these people, with this body, that took over from the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, the president of the Crisis Staff calls the meetings of the Crisis Staff. The secretary of the general assembly or a person authorised by the president takes the minutes of them. And sometimes I knew, but I did not have to know. I was dealing in finances. I was in charge of the maintenance of the building. I was involved in the joint affairs of all the organs. It's a huge task. I did not have to know about the meetings of the Crisis Staff, and especially not what decisions they made and how they were arrived at. I was never there to be able to know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: They were the only body that were meeting through that time, from the 13th of May onwards. You came under their authority. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was for a short period of time. You can see here the 13th of May. It was during the summer. I don't know when the Crisis Staff was disbanded. But as far as I remember, it didn't last that long. Maybe two or three months. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is the document that you were shown yesterday, and it's a decision of the war presidency dated the 23rd of July 1992. You said yesterday at page 51 of the LiveNote: "I never laid eyes on this decision before, nor have I ever heard about it, although it was talked about after the war. To be precise, in some recent contacts I had, I learned that a decision of this sort existed."

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did you first hear about this decision?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I heard of this decision sometime after the war. I heard that it had existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know -- I can't tell you that. In Celinac, there were rumours about the existence of such decision. After the war, this decision was not accepted very well by people who talked about it. But there were also others who said that this decision was indispensable, that it had to be adopted, because it provided for the protection of these people in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1999. Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman, page 28 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, could you go to the document which has the number 0326-2307 on the top. You can see there that these are minutes, handwritten minutes, of the 17th session of the Celinac Municipal Assembly held at 10.00 a.m. On the 28th of July 1992. It says that there were 51 assemblymen present; and apart from the assemblymen, it names other people who were also in attendance. The commander of the Celinac light infantry battalion, Janko Trivic; yourself, as joint affairs secretariat. Do you see your name there? Why did you say earlier that you never attended any Municipal Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason for me to say anything differently. I was the chief of the joint affairs department, and I attended some of the sessions to which I was invited in my capacity as the chief of this department. I don't remember a single word from this session. However, if it says here Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I attended as the chief of the joint affairs department, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will go through this document. But you were asked quite clearly this morning on a number of different occasions whether you attended any sessions of the Municipal Assembly. And you cat -- and you said that you didn't attend one session.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be honest. It was a long time ago. I'm not young myself. I have not made any notes. Everything there is is in my head, and it is possible that I was invited to attend a session in order to criticise me about the maintenance of the rooms in the building, about the cleaning of the premises, because that was what I did in my department. That was what my staff did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Round about this time, the 28th of July, who was the director of inland revenue in Celinac? Who was the director of inland revenue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, inland revenue. Do you have the B/C/S text of this document? Perhaps we can refer because I know that director of inland revenue is a typically English --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, on the same page that I took you to a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is inland revenue. There is also internal affairs or in-house affairs. I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Look, that document says -- mentions your name, Boro Mandic as being one of the persons present at that meeting. But your capacity is -- you read it out and tell us what it says. You were present there in your capacity as what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the head of department for joint affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that what the document says? Or does it say something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says SZP, which stands for the department of joint affairs, and that is exactly what I was. That is what the abbreviation stands for. May I please clarify while we are walking on this ground here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just a moment, to answer the Judge's question, the person named after you in relation to the revenue is Vlado Vrhovac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, I see. Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vlado Vrhovac, but not after me. That is a completely different department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. I understand. It's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The name appears after yours, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, while we are talking about this, may I please answer your question as to why I attended this particular session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 2 of the minutes, it says that the Municipal Assembly adopted resolutions on the location of building plots for the construction of garages. I participated in the bidding. I paid for the building plot that I was bidding for. And under (b), it says clearly that the Municipal Assembly issues resolutions. And under 1, it says Boro Mandic son of Djordje from Celinac. And as I as a natural person, and a buyer of this plot on which I was going to build a garage, I was supposed to be present at that session, and I, therefore, attended. Whether everybody else on this list attended, I don't know. This is what it reads under item (b) of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You wouldn't attend in your capacity as the chief of the joint office, no? I find it strange to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could have gone on both counts. It was not forbidden. It was a public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Are there any other minutes where the witness's name appears, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's find out what the reason was in each case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I take you to the agenda, which is still on page 03262307 for you, and it's on page 29 of the English translation. Basically, it was to adopt the minutes of the Municipal Assembly's 16th session held on the 13th of May 1992. And it was at the Municipal Assembly session held on the 13th of May that they adopted the decision to appoint members to the Crisis Staff. And so as you were attending this meeting, you would have had to have read the minutes of the 16th session of the 13th of May, would you not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a member of the assembly, and it was not my duty to read minutes because I have no say in decisions, nor do I have the right to vote. I could only attend in the capacity that I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I doubt that we would have had the right to have a copy of the minutes in any case. I don't know what the procedure was at the time, whether the minutes were read or taken as read. We'll move to something.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to take the witness through the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if we go to paragraph 6 also on the agenda, was the verification of decisions and solutions adopted by the Crisis Staff of the Celinac Municipality war presidency, and then it listed them from A to M. Now underneath that it says that this session was postponed until 8.00 a.m. on 5th of August 1992 because there wasn't a quorum. Is that correct? If you go to page numbered 0326-2311, and just above that --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it says so here, it must be true. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can move on to page 32 of the English translation -- 31, I'm sorry. That is the minutes of the 17th session of the Municipal Assembly held on the 5th of August 1992. It says the assemblymen that were present, and it says that the session was also attended by yourself. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on the agenda again, we have adopting the minutes of the 16th session held on the 13th of May 1992 and we also have as item 6 the verifications of the decisions and solutions adopted by the Crisis Staff. Now, sir, I want to take you to English translation pages 34 to 36. And in the B/C/S, it is ERN number 0326-2317 to 2320. We have there Major Ranko Trivic giving a political and security report on the situation in the Celinac Municipality. Do you have page 0326-2317? And we can see that Major Trivic says --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- A few lines after he begins: "There is sporadic fire and destruction of property, Muslim and Croatian homes, an increase in crime, car theft, destruction, arson. This is carried out by armed groups who do this in a planned way and are helped out by some politicians. This manifests itself through gatherings of extremists and support to such people which results in anarchy and ends in genocide being carried out." Do you know which politicians Major Trivic is referring to there?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that an accurate description of the destruction that was going on in relation to property belonging to Muslim and Croatian persons?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the month of July, then it is true. There was torching of Muslim houses, and we witnessed it. Most normal people condemned it, and we can see from this document that this major also condemns it and puts it to the session as a problem. But who organised it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
