utterances.text: Can you take you to page 0326-2319. We have Dusko Dzajic, chief of the SKB, in Celinac. And he says: In the Besici and Mehovci area, which is mostly populated by Muslims" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, for Your Honours and Mr. Ackerman, page 35 and 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- In the Besici and Mehovci area which is mostly populated by Muslims, we cannot guarantee their safety and we must take a political stand that will enable these people to move out the Muslims of the area. And further, in Celinac Municipality, none of the non-Serbs have weapons, so there are no problems there. But there are around ten armed Serbs who are causing trouble and they should have their weapons taken away." It says here that the non-Serbs had weapons [as said]. So what was the threat? You mentioned a moment ago that Muslim and Croatian property was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this was the month of July, it's not Dusko Dzajic, I want this corrected to Djajic. And the Muslim village was also misnamed. It is called Mehovci. It may have been recorded inaccurately or interpreted inaccurately. Since the war had already begun, I know that everyone feared everyone. Serbs kept guard around their villages, and so did Muslims. Fear was all-pervasive and ubiquitous, and as this chief of SUP Dusko Dzajic said, I believe that these were some renegade men who should have been prevented from continuing with their crime spree.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, just for the record, because the question itself does explain it. But line 14, page 4 to 6, you are quoted as having stated, Ms. Sutherland, it says here, this document in other words, that the non-Serb had weapons. Actually what the document says is that in Celinac municipality, none of the non-Serbs had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's what I thought you had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you had said, but the transcript says exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can I take you in the English translation to page 44, ERN number 0326-2332 in your language. Can you see there under item 7, Andjelko Topic, he has read the report on the work of the war presidency so far, and now all these decisions should be verified at the Municipal Assembly session. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it. Yes. Yes, yes. Andjelko Topic was the secretary of the assembly. He also led the Crisis Staff, or handled the Crisis Staff. So he had all these decisions in his possession. And when the conditions for normal work of the assembly would be created, then he would present all this, read it out, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were in attendance at this session on the 5th of August 1992 where Andjelko Topic reads the report on the work of the war presidency and asks that all these decisions now become -- now be verified. And then there's a discussion which follows on these decisions. Can I take you to - this is on page 46 of the English translation - can I take you to 0326-2335 in your language. We can see Ilija Maksimovic, and he says he mentioned the problem of moving the Muslims who want to leave the area. They should be given the possibility to do so without any incidents or problems. We should organise this so that these people can move out peacefully. The commission should assess all of this, and I will provide a certificate of having moved out of the AR Krajina. If you read further down that page - and for Your Honours, it's on page 46 of the English translation - and it's over the page for you, sir, Ljubo Aleksic, not all the Muslims mentioned in the decision are extremists. The real extremists should be exposed. A couple of people down, again, Ilija Maksimovic: As soon as the war operations in Kotor Varos end, the decision on the status of the non-Serbian population in Celinac Municipality will cease to be valid. Let us adopt the decision on Muslims moving out voluntarily. We should make it possible for those who voluntarily want to move out of Celinac Municipality to do so. Sir, although it's not specifically mentioned in its full title, they are discussing, are they not, Exhibit P1998 which was the decision of the war presidency of Celinac of the 23rd of July in relation to the status of non-Serbs, the document that you said you had never seen before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maksimovic refers to the title. The decision on the status of the non-Serbian population in Celinac Municipality. I think that's more than enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. It isn't mentioned as one of the decisions earlier, in the list of decisions, but it's discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I take you now -- I'm sorry, before we move on, you said in terms before, earlier today, that you had never seen that decision or heard of it until after the war.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is so, yes. As far as I remember, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You are in attendance at this meeting where it's being discussed.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to assure myself that you are understanding me correctly. I did not attend these sessions either as a recording secretary or a full-fledged deputy who had the background material in front of him. I would come and go as the chief of this joint affairs department who did -- who dealt with technical aspects of the work. I did not hear the entire discussion, and that's why I'm not in a position to comment. I have absolutely no recollection of any item of the agenda of this session, and especially not the discussion itself. I did not attend in any capacity which would allow me to hear all of this. But if it says so here, it must be true.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, we can see for a number of pages a number of different people discussing this document. It starts with Ilija Maksimovic, it goes on to Sveto Kovacevic, it goes on to Gojko Djuric, Ljubo Aleksic, Mirko Mikanovic, again Sveto Kovacevic, again Ilija Maksimovic --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- Mladen Savic, Aleksis Srdic, Ljubo Mrdjan, again Mirko Mikanovic, Irfan Tetaric.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sreten Radojkovic, Nedjo Babic, Milorad Stankovic, Mirko Mikanovic again, Radomir Trivic. Are you telling this Court that you knew nothing about this document where you were in attendance and all of these people and more have discussed this decision?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm telling this Court with perfect honesty is that I do not recollect the discussion on this item of the agenda. It is possible that I attended only the beginning of the session whereafter I came and went. And I don't remember the discussion, although reading this now and knowing the assemblymen, I believe that this is true. Their contributions were sincere and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. We will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I take Your Honours to page 48 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you turn to page 0326-2337, and we are Mirko Mikanovic. "This list should not have been made public. It should have been given to the military police so they could keep them under surveillance." On the next page, on page 49, Radomir Trivic, for you, this is on page 0236-2339 -- it should be publicly announced that the municipal assembly refuses to adopt this decision. This way we would avoid a political situation that could escalate and the police could keep the extremists under surveillance." I now want to take you - Your Honours, page 51. Sir, can you turn to page 0326-2342, Radomir Trivic said, or he suggests, that they do not vote on the decision because of the consequences in the international community. Now, sir, after that Braco Derajic says it is only common sense, allow people to go where they like. Sir, you are the next speaker, are you not? And this is what you say about the decision on the status of the non-Serbs. You provided an additional explanation of the decision. Where the list is concerned, it should be rated and placed in a more realistic framework. The obligations from this decision do not refer to loyal inhabitants of the municipality." Does that now refresh your memory as to the discussion that you were involved in on the 5th of August about this decision?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that session, and I can say this honestly before this Honourable Court, I attended, as it says in the beginning, in my capacity as chief of the joint affairs service with the responsibilities that that position implies. I had no special tasks. In view of this discussion that you summarised in which some people made one suggestion, other people made other suggestions, I wasn't probably aware of what decision it was exactly or what list they're talking about. I must have commented in light of the very accurate discussions of Irfan Trivic, Mirko Mikanovic, and others, and I must have said that there are many loyal citizens, and that that decision should be understood in a more fair way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you go to page 0236-2342. It states here that you were providing an additional explanation of the decision over and above what had been said before. You lied to the Court earlier when you said that you had not seen this decision before and you knew nothing about it until after the war, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that decision because I didn't draft it, nor did I participate in its enactment or adoption or enforcement, and I can not make any comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you participated in the discussion on that decision during the meeting of - I don't know when - according to these minutes. And you even provided an additional explanation of the decision. So on that day, I take it that you were very familiar with the decision itself already. Otherwise, you wouldn't have opened your mouth, especially as head of the joint unit or joint office which had nothing to do as such with this decision.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply don't remember. I did not participate in any of the bodies that adopted it or voted or made decisions, and what I may have said -- I was under no obligation to make any contribution. There was the secretary who presented this decision. Andjelko Topic invited discussion, and this may be a mistake on the part of the recording secretary who said that I provided an additional explanation. If I did say anything, it may have been just my opinion, my opinion to the effect that one needed to be more realistic in assessing, and take into account all the incidents that were taking place in the municipality, not only directed against the Muslims where perpetrators were Serbs, but probably other incidents where the situation was reversed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even if what you are saying now is correct, it would still contradict what you stated earlier; namely, that you never knew about this decision, about the subject matter of this decision, until after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say this again: I did not see this decision in writing and signed. I may only have heard the discussion to a limited extent because I came and went all the time during that session. I may have heard comments made by certain people. And I was always of the opinion that it was only right to protect some people because that was fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go back a little bit. First, you tell us that you never heard about this decision until much later. Never knew about the existence of this decision. There were rumours, you said. Then you are faced with the minutes of a meeting of the assembly in which you are given to understand that at a meeting -- at a meeting in which you were present, this decision was discussed. And you tell us maybe I was there, I don't know, as head of the joint office or joint department, and it was very normal that I would stay there for a while, and then leave. Maybe it took place after I had left, and that's why I don't know anything about it. Now that you are faced also with a part of the minutes that quotes you as discussing and giving your own additional explanation on the decision, are you suggesting that this may be a mistake of the secretary now, that you still don't remember anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember the decision. I really hadn't seen the decision before this. And I wasn't invited to attend as an MP. I did not vote. If I did take the floor at all, and I believe I did just to say these two sentences, then I could have said that I was not quite happy with some of the remarks of the previous speakers, and I was not happy to let these people be treated as they were treated. I was against that then as I am against it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which would mean, however, that you were fully aware what the subject matter of the discussion and, therefore, of the decision was. I know of no one except very few persons that take the floor and speak about things that they don't know about or that they know nothing about. There are a few.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that point in time when I happened to be there, most probably I realised what the debate was about. And in my contribution, I gave my support as a positive person to other positive people who debated in that way, and I repeat, that was Mr. Mikanovic, Radomir Trivic, and some other, Irfan Tetaric, who were not members of the Serbian democratic party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, if you had no right to speak, why did you speak and what were the additional -- what was the additional explanation that you provided? It's a compound question. First of all, why did you speak if you had no right to speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered that question. He wanted to give support to the people --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The people who took positive attitude, and the entire Celinac and Republika Srpska knew very well how I behaved during the war. And my wish was, although I wasn't entitled to speak, to give my support to people who thought otherwise. And about my conduct, anyone can ask every Muslim from Celinac how I behaved. It can take days for me to give you the list of people I helped, and if this is going into the public domain, to whom I offered help, whom I found a job, whom I did not dismiss from work, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I just want you to answer my question. What additional explanation did you provide at this session about this document?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None at all. But besides, the president of the assembly and the secretary who are authorised to give interpretation, there was no need for me in my capacity to support this decision and I truly believe, and I don't remember giving any additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this was an illegal discriminatory, persecutorial decision, and that's why you won't admit any involvement in it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, object to that characterisation. Many people have said it was a decision for the purpose of protecting those people, and there's even some indication in this discussion that that's the case. As soon as Kotor Varos's hostilities were over, they didn't need to be protected any longer. So I think that's just a bit of a submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, but the witness has already in part of his testimony gave the two sides of the coin on this decision. He said precisely what you said now, that some people considered it to be obnoxious, and others the way you described it. So I will allow the question. The witness is being asked whether he is claiming absolute noninvolvement in this decision because he acknowledges that it was discriminatory, obnoxious decision. So I allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite frankly, before this Honourable Court, I can state that I did not draft, write, create, saw, or voted upon this decision because it was impossible. I wouldn't repeat everything else, not to waste your time. What I said was said in the context of these positive debates because that was only logical. Whether the decision was a discriminatory one or not, now, when I read it as a lawyer, it is discriminatory on the one hand, when you look at the text and the language of it. But in those debates and in the public, there were rumours that those people should be protected because operations were in progress around the town, so in order to prevent those people from being killed at the time, this decision or part of the decision referring to this particular aspect was of temporary nature. And if that was true, that was a good decision. But that refers to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think you need to press this any further, Ms. Sutherland, and you move to something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. It can be given to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to the situation in Celinac Municipality. You said at page 56 of your testimony that you believed that during the period of time until Mr. Brdjanin stopped being president of the Executive Committee, that Celinac as a town neighbourhood was safe. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. And I stand by it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you residing in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May and June 1992, I was living in the centre of the town of Celinac in the building where my neighbours came from all ethnic communities. My one next-door neighbour was a Croat, and the other next-door neighbour was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you hear explosions and shooting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, during this same time frame?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May and June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, we can see here this is a script from Banja Luka Radio dated the 11th of June 1992. It talks about explosive devices being thrown into a Muslim house and three shops owned by Muslims, and that the damage to these establishments is extensive.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this you can see that this was a release broadcast by Radio Banja Luka. It doesn't show exactly how they came to gather this kind of information. But I personally know, because I was there with my wife and my children, and Celinac is a small place, one could hear explosions always at night. But whether all these incidents took place, I don't know. I know that the house of Ismet Beharic house was attacked. He was an acquaintance of mine. And another friend of mine with whom I was together in the military service --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you aware of these shops where explosive devices had been thrown?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean, after they had happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sabiha Hodzic, her shop, Sabiha Basic, and Salih Nezirovic.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, when dark falls, and most of the time we didn't have electricity, we all locked up ourselves until the morning. I never went out. But in the morning on my way to work, and I walked most of the time because we didn't have petrol, I saw some of these things, although I didn't see the house of Ismet Beharic, which is a bit farther away. But I did see that these shops were attacked with explosive devices.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you look now at Exhibit P1992. Sir, this is another Banja Luka Radio script dated the 12th of June 1992. And halfway down there, you will see in Celinac at 1.00 in the morning, one or more unknown perpetrators attacked the building of the mosque board with hand grenades. Again, did you hear this explosion or did you hear about this following this incident?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know concerning the mosque and its destruction, once we heard an explosion, and somebody said that the mosque had been demolished, which I personally saw while I was passing by the mosque, and I saw that it wasn't demolished. Whether there was an attempt to do that, I don't know. Sometime after that, we heard a powerful bomb or a powerful sound during the night. And in the morning, the whole of Celinac was able to see that an explosive had been planted at the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your answer would have been yes to both parts of the question, and we would have finished half a minute earlier. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the Celinac Municipality wasn't so safe for non-Serb residents, was it, just looking at these two exhibits here? You would agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you frankly that I didn't feel safe either, just like everybody else. My neighbours, Adila and Marija, we were all - and you can call them to testify to that - we were all afraid, and we felt the most safe when we were together. When I said that the municipality of Celinac, Celinac, and with this I meant the town of Celinac, in the previous period, two Muslim-populated villages were evacuated. They went to Banja Luka. And a number of those citizens resided with their families in Celinac because it was rather safe. There were no massive evacuations or expulsions, nor any major devastation until the very end of the war. I know a large number of people from these villages who had been evacuated who resided in Celinac. I saw them on a daily basis, and I socialised with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We got the answer. It was safe, but it wasn't. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn to a completely different topic, and that is the documents that you brought with you to The Hague. They are Documents DB170 to DB180.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First of all, who asked you to bring these documents to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody. Given the fact that I've come here not to be the witness either for the Prosecution or for the Defence, but to be the witness for the truth, I wanted to say that the ministry of construction where I work now and where I worked during the war, how it operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't answered the question actually. But anyway...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He has, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nobody asked you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you weren't asked, why did you want to bring them? You said that you wanted to say that the ministry of construction, how it operated.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It operated absolutely legally in compliance with the law, and that is how it works today. And if anyone should ask me, I do know what the subject was -- and if anyone should ask me how it operated during the war where Mr. Brdjanin was employed, that is how it worked. And the documents that were presented here from unknown sources, unknown to me, testify along these lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why did you pick these particular documents to show how the ministry operated?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you recall, I said yesterday that hundreds of such documents are in the ministry, and only one or two of these documents were taken from case loads that we resolved during the war. One refers to the exchange of residential areas, one refers to rationalisation, et cetera, et cetera. Well, I don't think that you can believe that there were only two or three people applying to the ministry of construction for help. You are free to look into the archives and records, and you can see for yourself how many decisions had been taken by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why these particular documents as opposed to others of the many hundreds that you have told us are there?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing particular about them. I took them randomly, just to illustrate that the Serbs, the Muslims, and the Croats had been treated in an equal manner. Even if there are people of other nationality, there was a man -- he was either Polish or an Austrian; I don't remember his name. But we didn't act in the ministry according to people's names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic. You said yesterday at page 53 of the LiveNote that an incident occurred in August 1992 which you said was very clearly etched in your memory. You said you believed --

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- It was in the beginning of August when persons were leaving the Celinac Municipality in buses parked outside the building, municipal building.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified at page 55, and I quote: "Mr. Brdjanin as a representative of the assembly of Republika Srpska and as a humanitarian, he used his authority in favour of the Muslim population of Celinac Municipality and asked the police to intervene on their behalf and disperse this unwelcome gang and for these Muslims to be placed somewhere safe." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So Mr. Brdjanin was a person of authority in Celinac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin as the deputy of the national assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the multiparty election in 1991, a huge number of votes, and he acted accordingly towards his voters, regardless of their nationality. He acted as a true deputy as it was his duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: My question was Mr. Brdjanin was a person of authority in the Celinac Municipality, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a person with authority because he had been working there for many years. He was a good manager, a good entrepreneur, and among the citizens of Celinac from all ethnic background, he was well liked.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Isn't it also the fact that he was a person in authority because of the positions that he held? He was a deputy in the Republika Srpska Assembly.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the Municipality of Celinac, and he was responsible primarily for the voters from Celinac. This is absolutely true. Very often, he voted for other parts of the republic, but he took good care for -- about the welfare of the citizens of Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was his authority as a deputy in the RS Assembly as president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, he had authority to be able to intervene over the police on behalf of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Crisis Staff did not exist in August of 1992. It ended July 17th, so he wouldn't have had the authority at this time as president of the Crisis Staff. So I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The evidence is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'll deal with this. Technically it's right, but Your Honours have heard evidence from a witness who went to a meeting in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, the fact that he was president of the Crisis Staff, did that in itself make him a man of authority in Celinac Municipality? Was he looked at as a man of authority, also because of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember any dates, and I don't like to remember dates, to make it quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Forget dates. But did the fact that he was known to be the president of the ARK Crisis Staff, at some point in time, make him look like a clown or as a man of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday, and I repeat this today: I don't think that Mr. Brdjanin took advantage of his position in order to make this humanitarian gesture. And what I think, that is the opinion shared by all the citizens of Celinac, including Muslims, and that is that Mr. Brdjanin made this humanitarian gesture first of all as a token of humanitarian attitude towards his Muslim neighbour. I don't want at this point to speak anything else about other things. I want to speak only about Celinac and the ministry in which I work. And what I'm certain about is the only thing that refers to where I worked and what I know personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he looked -- was he perceived as a political charlatan or as a man of authority, of political authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how people perceived him. I personally saw him as a man who is good at working as the president of the Executive Committee within the scope of the committee's responsibility. As to what kind of politician he was, you may not believe me, but I never attended any of the rallies or have I ever -- well, practically we didn't have electricity for three years. We couldn't watch television. We were in a kind of information blackout. And what Mr. Brdjanin did publicly outside the municipality of Celinac, I cannot say anything. I didn't go to any of the rallies, and I didn't read newspapers because all the newspapers were publishing untruthful information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're beating around the bush and going around in circles in my opinion, because you're trying to shy away from even the idea proposed to you that Mr. Brdjanin was perceived as a man in power, as a man of authority. What do you have to say to that? Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brdjanin was a respectable person in his opportunity as a deputy and as a citizen. I deeply believe that as well as many people from Celinac believe. But as from the position of authority, I cannot say. I told you yesterday, I didn't see Mr. Brdjanin on the day when this unpleasant incident happened that provoked this incident afterwards. But from the position of his being acquainted, well acquainted with his Muslim neighbours, he acted in this context of these good relations, at least with the majority of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still going around in circles. Ms. Sutherland, I give him back to you. And we have got two minutes before the break. How much longer do you expect you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Half an hour, maximum, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You might as well start preparing the next witness. Do you want to break now? Two minutes from now we need to break. Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've mentioned a number of times that Mr. Brdjanin is a humanitarian. What is it about him that makes him -- that makes you say that he's a humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just say a few words, and that is what I know about him. When he was on the Executive Committee of Celinac Municipality, whoever came with any appeal to him, regardless of their ethnicity, he helped them. So if you are willing to accept my claim about this case of Celinac, then it is evident. When he worked at the ministry of construction, and I can specifically speak about that, roughly speaking, to all of us lower-ranking officers, he ordered and asked us to take care that no one who comes to the ministry is rejected and denied help. We complied with that even when he was away. There are living witnesses, there are documents about that. And in that context, I believe that in the way how he treated people who came to the ministry and how he treated the citizens of Celinac, he was a humanitarian. Outside of the scope of work of these organs, I was not participating there, and I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so as far as you're concerned, he's never shown any discriminatory feelings towards non-Serbs at all.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the ministry of construction, we only did jobs within the scope of our responsibility. Anyone can confirm that who had contacts with the ministry. Any other meetings and other things that took place did not occur on the premises of this ministry, and I know nothing about them. Well, anyway, the government sessions were held in Pale, and all other major organs were situated in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In respect to the Celinac Municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to break now, Ms. Sutherland. Actually what the witness is saying is that a husband can be held to be a good husband based on what he does at home, and regardless of his conduct outside. So let's take it up from there. Think about what I have just said, and you will have another barrage of questions waiting for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I hope you've thought about what I told you. Stop beating around the bush. Stop going around in circles. Answer the question straight yes, no, the way you know it. But don't give us or don't answer the questions that are put to you by giving information. You're not the only smart guy here, you know. I mean, it's... Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be shown Exhibits DB170 through DB180, the documents that he provided. If Mr. Mandic could be provided with all of them at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is better, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you point out for the Court those decisions that you say are signed by Mr. Brdjanin. Sir, the signature block, but those that have also been actually signed by Mr. Brdjanin. And if you could just read the exhibit number at the top of the page. I don't want to go into any detail relating to the actual exhibit. I just need you to give the Court the exhibit numbers of those documents that you say are signed by him.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin signed the enactment number DB172B dated the 1st of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. If you can continue.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another enactment, DB173B, dated 28th December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Please continue. Sorry. I should...

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subject DB175B, dated 19 December 1994. DB177B, dated 16th March 1993. DB178B, dated 9th December 1994. DB180B, dated 2nd November 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Brdjanin physically signed each one of those exhibit numbers that -- those documents that you have just read out, the exhibit numbers of?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with all of those documents. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1697.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, this is a newspaper article from the Washington Post. The author is Jonathan Randall. The dateline of the article is the 10th of February 1993. Can I take you -- can you look, please, at the paragraph which starts "Bosnian Serb housing administrator Radoslav Brdjanin...," if you can look please at the page numbered 0304-4494 in your language. And it's the last paragraph on that page. Sir, I'll read the paragraph for you: "Bosnian Serb housing administrator Radoslav Brdjanin, an avowed radical Serb nationalist, said he,`personally argued that those unwilling to defend [Bosnian Serb territory] must be moved out', but that the Serb political leadership so far had not agreed. He said he believes the `exodus' of non-Serbs should be carried out peacefully, so as to `create an ethnically clean space through voluntary movement.' Muslims and Croats he said `should not be killed, but should be allowed to leave -- and good riddance.'" Whilst you were working with Mr. Brdjanin at the ministry, did he ever express any sentiments like that to you?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This, if Mr. Brdjanin indeed said it, and I'm not aware that he did, could be an expression of political sentiments. But certainly not in his position as minister. I personally did not hear him say anything like that. And we never discussed it. I never wished to discuss such issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you look now two paragraphs down from the one I just read you, read out to you, the paragraph starting, and I will read it to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The paragraph starting: "Specifically, Brdjanin said he is preparing laws to expel non-Serbs from government housing to make room for 15.000 Serb refugees and for Serb combatants' families. With that in mind, he said, officials recently began measuring Muslim apartments to ensure that each resident occupied no more than 12 to 15 square metres." And these sentiments are echoed by the person you say is a humanitarian.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of his statement. But such laws had never been prepared or enacted in the ministry of construction. And as for this statement, I don't know that he made it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I've finished with that document. I would now like you to watch a short video. It's Exhibit P509.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the video could be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Brothers and sisters, citizens of the Krajina and all the other patriots who have come to this gathering, we must not be tricked by this greatest of trickeries into believing we are voting for peace or war. We are voting for the betrayal of the salvation of Republika Srpska. The leftists who are offering us again to live together must know that the obligation of the Serbs for the next 100 years is to wipe their shoes of this non-Christian scum who are tarnishing our lands. "Moreover, it is not true that we do not know where our borders lie. Our borders lie from Benkovac to Trebinje."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our borders lie from the Hungarian border all the way down to Sokolac, with Belgrade" --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Stop the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, who would be the non-Christian scum that Radoslav Brdjanin was referring to in that clip?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably Bosniak Muslims, and communists, socialists.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After viewing that videoclip, do you still say that Mr. Brdjanin's a humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously a recording made at a rally which I did not attend either from the podium or from the audience. But my entire testimony refers to the territory of the Celinac Municipality and Celinac town. I cannot speak to anything else. These words are not nice, but I have heard very few of them because I did not attend rallies, and I did not follow the reporting of the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have one final question: You mentioned earlier in your testimony that you didn't want to have anything to do with any of the Crisis Staff, either the Krajina staff or the Celinac Crisis Staff. Was this because you knew that those bodies were responsible for the crimes that were committed in Celinac and within the Autonomous Region of Krajina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have a very clear position on this issue, which I voiced at the beginning of my yesterday's testimony. I did not belong to the Serbian democratic party. I did not belong to any narrow circle of any organ. I did not wish to attend their meetings. Quite simply speaking, I was not a desirable member in any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you haven't answered my question. My question was why did you say you didn't want to have anything to do with either the regional Crisis Staff or the Celinac Crisis Staff? What was it about those bodies that you didn't like?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it mostly had to do with the fact that the majority of the members of these bodies were from the Serbian democratic party. I have never been a member of that party myself, and I have no love lost for it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a very simple reason: When the multiparty system prevailed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I, as a reasonable person, realised that the ruling parties, SDS, HDZ, and SDA, were based on ethnicity, and that they realised this themselves, and they immediately started carrying out policies which I didn't agree with and have no compassion for, which is still the case today. That is the only and very simple reason. This is how I conduct myself under the present system as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who did you say was carrying out these policies, the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those policies were implemented by all national or ethnic-based parties, SDS, SDA, and HDZ, each in its own territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago that you had no love for the SDS. I want you to expand on why that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Love lost, the way it was termed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's simply a set phrase in our language. Anyway, I'm not on good terms with them primarily because, as I said yesterday in the beginning of my testimony, that this party did not accept me from the outset because I was not a member.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But I still don't think you've answered the question. Why did you not want to have any involvement with the Crisis Staffs, either Celinac Crisis Staff or the regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was made up for the most part of members of the SDS. They were the majority. I don't know the exact figures, but I believe they were the majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was these -- these members of the SDS who were carrying out the ethnic cleansing, both in Celinac and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Autonomous Region of Krajina, I cannot speak to that. I can only speak to the Celinac Municipality. People were moving out, and you saw the minutes and the records of sessions yourself. Whether it was voluntary transfer where people moved out at their own will and without any incidents involved or whether they moved out because they forced, I'm not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Why were they leaving their homes that they had lived in for many, many years of their own volition? Why would that many people want to leave?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: I know a lot of Serbs who left that area who went to live abroad or to Serbia. To cut a long story short, people were running away from the war. They were running away from poor living conditions. We did not have electricity for three years. We had no food or detergents. And even those people who stayed on did not have an easy time of it. Everybody suffered from the war and from the living conditions during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was the Muslims that were leaving because of the policies to drive them out, was it not?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, I see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I looked at you. Can I know what questions you want to -- go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at -- I'd like you to be given back P1999, please. And the page I want to refer you to in your language is 03262337?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In English, Your Honour, it's on page 48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, I asked you about a Muslim director of a primary school by the name of Irfan Tetaric. There's an Irfan Tetaric on this page. Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the contention is that what's being discussed here is the decision on the status of the non-Serbian population of the Celinac Municipality, which is on P1998. If we look at what Mr. Tetaric says, if it's referring to this decision, what he says is it will be a shock to the entire Muslim population, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, if you ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't that an indication that the decision has not been issued, that it will be a shock but apparently has not yet been issued? Is that what he's saying there?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask Mr. Ackerman not to lead in future in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are right. Mr. Ackerman, you know that -- I think you ought to rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you think it means when he says "the decision will be a shock to the entire Muslim population" with regard to whether or not that decision has been issued?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here in the B/C/S version: "This document is a shock" which probably means that it was adopted by that time. But it also says that Muslims should be allowed to move out unless they have served in the enemy army. That's what it says in these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is a -- Irfan Tetaric apparently is a deputy, is he, of the assembly at this time. And I think we're in July or August of 1992. Is he still serving as a deputy of the assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORO MANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irfan Tetaric said this at an assembly session, and I believe he was deputy. I was not the speaker of the assembly, so I cannot say this with any certainty. But I do believe that he was an assemblyman, an MP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I'm sure on the same page, you will notice that this was the process of verification of the decision. In fact, if you refer to a few lines up, you will see that the assembly members were being asked to verify or not to verify a decision. Anyway, do you have any questions? Do you have any questions? I just have one question. Were you ever a member of the league of communists or a member of the communist party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you allow me just a few words on this issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you would be one of those non-Christian scum, a member of that community, no, according to yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a very good student, in the third year of secondary school, I was admitted into the League of Communists and continued as a member until the first multiparty elections. But I was always just an ordinary member. I didn't have any other functions, not even small ones like treasurer. And after that, I was never a member of any other party, and I decided firmly never to become one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Which brings us to an end and which also brings me to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. You will now be escorted out of this courtroom by our usher, who will extend to you all the assistance you require to enable you to return to your home country. I thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Honourable Trial Chamber for enabling me to testify because I have come to tell the truth, and not to be either a Prosecution or a Defence witness. And I thank the people from the Prosecution for their fair treatment and conduct of the Prosecution, and I thank everybody in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. And travel safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, are we ready for the next witness? We deal with the preliminaries at least?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: He's present, Your Honour. I'm ready to go forward if the Court is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make use of these 15, 17 minutes that we have. There are no protective measures, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There are no protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we're talking of Branko Cvijic. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've noticed that, and we are taking steps ourselves to question people about this, but I noticed that VWS is putting our witnesses in the same witness room here together. So they could speak to each other. But we have told them absolutely not to do that, not to speak to each other. I think a question from the Court or something like that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I will do it quietly after the sitting, Mr. Ackerman. I thank you for bringing this to my attention. Registrar and Elena, we get to this after the sitting, need to bring this... They should know better. Yes, the next witness, please. Mr. Ackerman, if there is any witness coming and that we need to caution on our part of any rights not to answer any --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd let you know, Your Honour, if there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. I don't know, because I know very little about the background of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. You are going to give -- start giving evidence. We won't finish today. We finish tomorrow, I hope. And before you do so, our regulations, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony, you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth, and nothing about the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is being handed to you now. Please take it in your hands, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please, take a seat. You have been summoned to give evidence by the accused in this case which basically means that you are going to be first examined, asked a set of questions by the Defence team. Is it you, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's Mr. Cunningham who is co-counsel for Mr. Brdjanin who will be examining you in chief. He will then be followed by Mr. Nicholls from the Prosecution team. But that will be tomorrow, I suppose. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your name is Branko Cvijic, correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you questions, and I would like you to listen very carefully to the question I ask you, and just answer the question that's asked. If we need additional explanations, additional informations, additional information from you, either His Honour or myself or the other lawyer when appropriate will ask. Is that fair enough? Do you understand those instructions?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you tell us your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of August, 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in what municipality were you born?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I was born in a village between the municipalities of Prijedor and Banja Luka. The name of the village is Krivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in what municipality do you now live?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I now live in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long have you lived in the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I have lived in the municipality of Banja Luka since 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I would like for you to tell the Chamber about your educational background starting with where you attended secondary school; and if you attended university, where, and what degrees you might have.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I finished high school in Prijedor, then enrolled and graduated from the law school in Zagreb in 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you pass your bar exam after graduation from the law faculty?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I passed two exams. One for administration, and the other was a judicial or bar exam with which in our country you can serve both as a judge or as an attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Briefly, and when I say briefly, I do mean briefly, tell us about your educational experience with respect to administration or administrative law.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: After I graduated in 1964, I got a job with the Municipal Assembly of Koprivnica. It's a town near Zagreb where I worked for six years. In 1972 I moved back to my birthplace in Banja Luka where I worked for seven years. Then I worked for nine years in a construction company. And then at the Rudi Cajavec electrical company. And then again in 1991 in January of that year, I was appointed secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka where I worked until 1998. In that year, I moved to a bank by the name of Vojvodina Bank, with a branch office in Banja Luka, which in the meantime became a highly reputable and solid bank. And the majority owner, stockholder, is an LHB bank from Frankfurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we are going to have the same problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If I might try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- I would prefer if I leave the control of the witness in your hands rather than me having to tell the witness you're going around in circles, you're beating around the bush, you're telling us a lot of information which we don't need. Try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, please -- and I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, please listen to my question. It's a simple one. I just wanted to know about your educational experience with respect to administrative law or administration. We can talk about your employment experience later, just focus on that. Did you attend a university course or specialised training in the area of administrative law or administration?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. These are the subjects taught at the faculty of law. But I didn't pass any particular exams for working in administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So in addition, I take it - and I might have the Court's permission to lead briefly on this - with respect to your training in municipal administration, you got that experience while serving in the town near Zagreb and while working for the municipality of Banja Luka. Am I correct on those two points, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I take it from your testimony you worked for the municipality of Banja Luka on two separate occasions, and those two separate occasions were interrupted --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: -- Were interrupted when you worked for the construction company. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Listen carefully: When was the first time period when you worked for the municipality of Banja Luka? What years are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: From 1972 until 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Briefly, and again I emphasise the word briefly, during that six-year period from 1972 until 1978, what were your duties?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I was an expert associate for bylaws. And at one time, between 1974 and 1978, I was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. The company that you worked for, was that a construction company? And I believe you would have started that in 1979. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: It was a construction company, and I got an employment there in May 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And during your employment with that company, did you come to know, meet, Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, Radoslav Brdjanin worked in one of the departments of this company in Celinac. He was a technical director of a small unit which was part of that bigger company.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And since that time that you worked for that company, have you remained an acquaintance, a friend of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Up until 1976, I knew him. We worked in the same company. We did not socialise. We didn't visit each other's homes. In 1986, we spent a year in Algeria in the town Ersaf near Oran, and we got close together. So when we went back to our country, we did meet more frequently than before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, I want to just briefly because we're going to take a break in a minute, after you worked for that construction company, you went back to work for the municipality of Banja Luka. Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: In the meantime, I worked for three years for the Rudi Cajavec company in Banja Luka, and then I went back to my job in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And the second term you spent with the municipality, how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Since 1991, January 1991, until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in those seven years or so that you spent during your second term, briefly in the one minute that we have remaining, tell us your job title or job titles for the municipality.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I had just one office, and that was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a good time to break if the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Sir, we have to stop here because our time limit is over. We will start again or we will continue tomorrow morning -- no, this afternoon, this afternoon at 3.00. I hope that give you enough time to rest a little bit and have a decent lunch. And then we hope to finish with you tomorrow morning. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham, while we wait for the witness, just to put us in a position to regulate the timetable --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm at a position to discuss that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you think your in-chief will last, your direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If he answers my questions as he was towards the end, I think I will be done in less than two hours. Mr. Nicholls and I have talked about his cross-examination, and I know that this will break the interpreters' hearts and the staff's heart, but he would ask to start his cross-examination tomorrow. Knowing that full well he could probably -- he can speak to this better I can, but the intimation I got was he would be done before noon, if he started at 9.00 tomorrow with his cross in the morning. And in light of the fact that we don't have any more witnesses scheduled here. It's up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's definitely up to the Court, but we try to accommodate you as much as we can. But the understanding would be, Mr. Nicholls, that you will finish the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Most definitely, Your Honour. I guess I have something over an hour, between an hour and two hours, depending on how it goes. So I would definitely finish tomorrow. But if Mr. Cunningham goes until sometime after 5.00, I'm pretty sure I wouldn't finish in the scheduled time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's proceed. And the understanding is that you start your cross tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you both. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I again want to remind you, sir, as you were doing towards the end of my examination, please listen to the question, answer directly only the question that I've asked, if I need any additional information I will ask for it. So thank you for direct answers towards the end of my examination. You are now working at a bank. Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how long have you been with that bank? How many years?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Five and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what is your job title at that bank?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Executive manager of the bank for legal and personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask you about political parties, and this question has a very bad connotation in my country, but I must ask it. Are you now or have you ever been a member of the communist party?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Now, I am not a member of any party, but I used to be a member of the communist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were you also a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the SDS for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And what was that certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: From 1990 until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to take you back to your first term with the municipality of Banja Luka. During the time that you spent with the municipality of Banja Luka in the 1970s, were you involved or was the municipality involved in a voluntary regional association situated in and around the municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. In 1973 or 1974, the community of municipalities of Banja Luka was formed made up of eight municipalities. And I was the secretary of that association.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What form was that association, was that a political body, economic body? Describe that very briefly for the Court.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: That was on an exclusively economic basis. That was a body that coordinated economic development in the areas of member municipalities in the associations so as to avoid overlapping of economic facilities, but rather according to the available natural resources of each municipality, and also for participating in joint projects, in road construction, waterworks, electrical network. And one of the most important issues at the time was the construction of the Banja Luka airport. There were no political connotations to the association.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Was this a -- which municipalities besides Banja Luka were involved in this voluntary association?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Laktasi, Gradiska, Srbac, Prnjavo, Celinac, Kotor Varos, and Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to relate this association to the -- the association of municipalities we saw in the 1990s, but with respect to that organisation in the 1970s where you served as the secretary, could the representatives from the different municipalities, could they pass a measure, a law, approve a project on their own, or did they need the approval of another body?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I already said that we had a coordinating role. Therefore, no binding enactments or laws could have been passed or bylaws or any executive decisions. We only made agreements and coordinated things. However, specific decisions were adopted by the respective assemblies of these municipalities that were members of the association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, before you proceed. Just for the record, page 86, line 6, amongst the municipalities that the witness mentioned, he also mentioned Celinac. That doesn't show up in the transcript, and goes for the record on now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So just to the record is clear, sir, could a project be finalised without the consent and approval of each of the Municipal Assemblies of the member municipalities?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In the early 1990s, did you become aware of another voluntary regional association of municipalities in and around Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. In the spring of 1992, I think it was in April, an Autonomous Region of Krajina was formed, and the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly adopted this decision as a member of this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want you to listen again to my question because you gave us a lot more information than I requested, and I'm not trying to criticise you, but just try to listen and we can get done a lot quicker. You've talked about the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Were you aware of the association of municipalities of the Bosanska Krajina that was the predecessor to that?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how it was called, but I think its name was the Autonomous Region of Krajina or Bosanska Krajina. I cannot say precisely, but either of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like to have, with the Usher's assistance, show you an Exhibit, P2354. I think it has already been pulled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You have that document in front of you. It's entitled: "Statute of the association of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina."

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, that was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Were you aware of this organisation in the early 1990s when you were in your position in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I don't think that it -- the association of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina existed in the 1990s. But rather, the association of municipalities of Banja Luka. I don't know whether the name was this because I hadn't been in the administration for a long time before that, and therefore I was not very much interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What I want you to do is I'd like you to turn to that page of that exhibit, Exhibit 2354, that contains Article 35 because I'm going to ask you questions based on your experience as a lawyer and your experience in administrative matters regarding municipalities. If you come -- when you find Article 35, I'd like for you to take the time to read it. It's two paragraphs, and I want you to read both paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just be clear for the record. This isn't being offered as expert testimony I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I said thank you, Mr. Nicholls; thank you, Mr. Cunningham, and I apologise for not having the microphone on. Yes, can we have the document on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Hold on just a second. I want to make sure you've read both paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So my first question is have you read both paragraphs in Article 35?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier you told us that with respect to the association that you worked for as the secretary in the 1970s, a decision was not binding on that organisation unless and until the member municipalities adopted it. Looking at the second paragraph of Article 35, is this second paragraph consistent or inconsistent with your experience with voluntary associations in the 1970s?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, this paragraph 2 exactly speak of what I was telling before, which means that the assemblies of these associations could not adopt binding decisions that would only come into effect once they would been approved and adopted by the assemblies of member municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like you to look at now at Article 1, the very, very first article, and I'd like for you to see if your municipality, Banja Luka, is contained within Article 1. Take the time to read it before you answer, please.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I see that Banja Luka Municipality is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, when you read Article 1, did you also see any indication whether this was a mandatory or a voluntary association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: It was an exclusively voluntary organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at Article 10, I'd like for you to look at that, now. Read it to yourself. And then once you're done reading, I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Does Article 10 support your statement that this was a voluntary association?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When did you become aware of the formation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I cannot say it precisely, but when that was offered as a proposal to the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka for adoption, I was then the secretary. It was put on the agenda. There was a debate by the deputies, and the decision was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Would that have been close to the beginning of your term that went from 1991 to 1997, or close to the end? Would it be in the early 1990s, mid-1990s, or late 1990s?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: In the early 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If I could have the usher show the witness Exhibit P81, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If you'll look at the second page, above the signature block for the president, it should show a date of 16 September 1991. Is that date consistent with your recollection of when you became aware of the ARK or the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer, but I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Look at Article 1 of Exhibit P81 and read that document -- read that article to yourself because I'm going to ask you a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if we were given -- we may have been given a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You were. We emailed it to Ms. Gustin last night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, but there's no larger list now. Okay, so that's the only list, because that only had three exhibits on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There should be the new DB exhibit as well that you and I talked about during the break. And if I might address him directly, Your Honour, just to assist him, I think it's going to be P2330, 81, 2354, which we've already gone through, and 227, decision 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, have you had a chance to read Article 1 of Exhibit P81, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
