utterances.text: Based on that, does this Autonomous Region of Krajina appear to be a successor to the alliance or association of Bosanska Krajina Municipalities that we discussed before?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this decision. I have never seen this language before in my life. And I don't understand and I can't comprehend Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now, during the time that you were in the 1990s -- you were the secretary for the Municipal Assembly in Banja Luka. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, did you have -- you became aware of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. We already know that. Now, here's my question, during the time period --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the early 1990s, specifically during 1991 and 1992, did the Autonomous Region of the Krajina have legislative power over the municipalities that were members of it?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No, it did not. It never had any legislative powers; rather, all the decisions taken by the AR Krajina had to be verified by Municipal Assemblies. And only after that could they come into force.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: How does that compare with your experience with the voluntary associations in the 1970s? Is it the same or is it different?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: The practice was the same, only the time frames were different, and situations were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk to you about the fact that in the early -- in 1991 and 1992, that there were Crisis Staffs or war presidencies formed in municipalities. With respect to Banja Luka, did your municipality form either a war presidency or a Crisis Staff during 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: In 1991, sometime in September, the war presidency of Banja Luka Municipality was established. And then in April -- it was operational until January 1992. Between January and April, there was nothing, and then in April the Crisis Staff of Banja Luka Municipality was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My questions are going to be dealing with the first war presidency. Tell us again when that was formed, what month, if you can recall.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I believe that this was either in September or October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And were you a member of the war presidency of Banja Luka, the first one?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I was not aware of the fact that I was a member. However, the investigators of this Tribunal showed me a document with my name on it as a member of this body in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you ever attend any meetings of this body in 1991?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: As for the sessions which considered issues that pertained to the authorities of the assembly, I attended those sessions. I didn't attend any other sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And based on the sessions that you attended, could you tell this Chamber what the primary function of that first war presidency was. What were they dealing with?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: The main function was looking after the population and especially the population of the Western Slavonia which started fleeing from that area and coming into the region of Banja Luka. And also, there was an immediate threat of war spreading across Bosnia and on towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. Measures were being taken in order to prepare for the normal functioning, normal life, normal provisions, normal supply of food, water, and electricity, and to preserve law and order in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the time that the first war presidency was in existence, was the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka still meeting, holding sessions?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. The Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka held regular sessions. I don't think that they skipped even one, so they continued working normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about the Crisis Staff. I believe you testified that that was formed on or about January of 1992. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. The Crisis Staff was not established in January, but in April. In mid-April or in late April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I showed you Prosecutor's Exhibit 81 which established the proclamation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the formation of the ARK 16 September 1991. So obviously, the second Crisis Staff was formed afterwards, after this September 1991 event. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina was established in April. I cannot be sure of that. I believe that this was in April, and that before that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't want you to speculate about when an organisation was formed. If you're not sure, don't speculate. But let me ask you this: Were you a member of the second Crisis Staff, the one that was formed in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. I was not a member of either the Banja Luka Crisis Staff or the ARK Crisis Staff. I was not a member of any of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you know someone by the name of Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And at this time period, in April of 1992, what was his position within the Municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: He was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And by virtue of that position, did he become a member of the Banja Luka -- the municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the municipal Crisis Staff, and also its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I take it because of your position as the secretary, that you worked closely with Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption. What I would like for you to do is very, very briefly describe to this Chamber what your duties were as the president -- I'm sorry. As the secretary.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: My basic duties were as follows: To prepare sessions of the Municipal Assembly, to monitor the legality of its work and the decisions which were proposed by the Executive Board. It was my task to study them and see whether they were legal or not. I was also in charge of calling the sessions, contacting the assemblymen, attending sessions, and doing everything necessary to provide for the technical functioning of the Municipal Assembly and its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in doing those duties, did you have a professional relationship with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: What do you mean by a "professional relationship"? I don't know what it means. In any case, we were both civil servants, and we cooperated rather closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you bring up a good point; it was a bad question. By virtue of your duties, were you in daily contact during the work week with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. Almost daily. There were days when we didn't meet, but as a rule we would meet every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, during the course of any of these meetings or through any other means, did you find out that Mr. Radic had been appointed to the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radic, by virtue of his position as president of the Municipal Assembly, became a member of the municipal -- of the ARK Krajina Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And where did the ARK Crisis Staff hold its meeting at?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: It held its meeting in the same building where the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka was; that is, in our building on the second floor in a separate, rather large office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you personally, do you have the recollection of ever attending any meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I didn't attend any meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Based on your daily work with Mr. Radic, do you know if he ever attended any meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: At the beginning, he did. I'm sure of that. Whether he was a regular member, a regular attendant of those meetings or not, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you know if he was ever sanctioned for ever failing to attend a meeting?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I don't know whether he ever suffered any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussions about the ARK Crisis Staff with Mr. Radic? That calls for a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Could you tell otherwise what his attitude was towards the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Well, on several occasions, I saw him being dissatisfied, even outraged as he came out of these sessions. In simple words, at times he was angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did he ever express to you what he was angry about?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. It was simply not his custom to talk about the things that went on at these sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk about the interaction, if any, between the ARK Crisis Staff and the Municipality of Banja Luka in 1991 -- excuse me, in 1992. It has been suggested that the ARK Crisis Staff was the highest governmental authority in the Krajina. I would like to know what your perception was of the ARK Crisis Staff. Was it a competent organ that could bind its members?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was not the highest organ of government in Krajina. It was not even the assembly because even the assembly had to submit all of its decisions for ratification to municipalities. So if the assembly was not the highest body, then the Crisis Staff consequently couldn't be that either. I don't know what else I should say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to make sure that I understand you correctly because the translation reads, on line 16: "So if the assembly was not the highest body, then the Crisis Staff subsequently couldn't be that either." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now by your answer, you seem to be suggesting that the Crisis Staff had some authority to order the member municipalities around. Was that the case? Was it considered a competent organ with the ability to order member municipalities around?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I personally didn't perceive the Crisis Staff in that way. The Crisis Staff in Banja Luka never ordered anything to the municipality of Banja Luka. It never proposed any issues for discussion. Nothing that pertained to the work of the Crisis Staff was ever discussed by the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your answer is a little unclear, and it's because of the poor question that I asked. I want you to focus in on the ARK Crisis Staff. Those that either were on the Banja Luka Crisis Staff or you, that worked in conjunction with members of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff, did you consider the ARK Crisis Staff to be a competent organ that could issue binding decisions by itself upon municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this point about the question asking him to comment about what other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- Other members of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff of which he said he was not a member, of the ARK Crisis Staff. He can give his opinion, but without some foundation, I don't think he can give an opinion of another Crisis Staff that he himself was not a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If I may interject, I tried to tie it in based on his dealings with the members of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're perfectly right, Mr. Cunningham. I think you're perfectly right. Go ahead and answer it the question. I think you've answered it already, but I don't know if it has made it to the... Yeah, it has. "It couldn't," he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your capacity as the --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I still believe that this Crisis Staff could not issue orders, could not make any decisions with the effect of an order. And the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka never had any such orders issued by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you in your capacity or based on your discussions with any member of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff ever become aware of any ARK Crisis Staff decisions or conclusions being considered by the Banja Luka Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I never learned of any such thing. Nobody ever informed me about any such thing, so I wouldn't be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your role as secretary, would you have been reading the minutes of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff? Would you have been reviewing documents that had been issued by the Banja Luka Municipal Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. That was not in my purview. I didn't attend their meetings. I did not need to look at their materials. They were not even accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: As far as you know, was there ever any ARK decision or conclusion that was ever implemented in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Not at the Municipal Assembly meeting. Whether it happened at the Executive Board or the Crisis Staff, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But based on what you just said, at the Municipal Assembly meetings, there was never anything that was adopted to the best of your recollection. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I would like with the usher's assistance to show the witness Prosecutor Exhibit 227. And I ask that it be opened to decision number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like for you to read that to yourself; specifically, read paragraph 1. What I'd like for you to do, if you feel it necessary, read all eight sections, but I'm only going to be asking you about paragraph number 1.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I've read the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now, reading this document, which is the conclusion of the Crisis Staff reached on 26 May 1992, in this document, it appears to me that the ARK Crisis Staff declares itself to be the highest organ of authority in the Krajina. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. But the Crisis Staff could not proclaim themselves to be that. It could not ascribe to itself higher authorities than the assembly. I've already said that, and I reconfirm it. So to my mind, this conclusion has no legal effect whatsoever. I have not seen it ever before, and the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka never received this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just because the ARK Crisis Staff says it's the highest organ of authority in the ARK, did that make it so?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. Anybody could proclaim themselves to be whatever they wanted to be. But the authorities were the authorities, and it was very well known who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I understand you say that you've never seen this document during your tenure in 1992 with Banja Luka. But let's just assume back in 1992 that you would have seen this. Would this conclusion have led you in your position as secretary to the assembly, would you have suddenly said "oh, this is different"? Would you have recognised this?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I would say that this was nonsense, and I would go to Mr. Radic and I would ask for the annulment of this thing as something that is illegal, that is against the law, and that is simply impossible. However, I didn't know of any such thing, so I didn't ask for any corrections or amendments.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you were in Banja Luka, and understanding that you did not attend the Crisis Staff -- the Municipal Crisis Staff meetings, let me ask you this: Did the Banja Luka Municipal Crisis Staff have the competence, the authority, to issue binding orders, first of all, to the police?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. No. No. It never had any competence over the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: With respect to, again, the Municipal Crisis Staff, would it have had the competence, the authority, to issue binding orders to military?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No chance. Both the military and the police were always independent at the level of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Based on your understanding of the ARK Crisis Staff, could the ARK Crisis Staff somehow issue binding orders to the military and/or the police?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No. The ARK Krajina Crisis Staff could not issue any orders either to the police or the army. And both the army and the police were way above any of these two Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you say "way above," briefly tell us what you mean.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: What I mean is that at the level of the republic, there was a government. And the government had its Ministry of the Interior. So nothing that pertained to the military or the police could pertain to the authority of either any of the municipalities or any of the Crisis Staffs. The army had its supreme command at the level of the state, and everything that happened in the army went down along a vertical command line.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to remind you that -- the interpreters are doing a great job, but they may be struggling to stay up with you when you talk so fast, so please remember to slow down a little bit if you can. Some have suggested that there was a change in the law of internal affairs that somehow gave the --

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me re-ask the question. Some have suggested that there was a change in the law of internal affairs that somehow empowered the Crisis Staffs such as the ARK Crisis Staff to issue binding orders to the military and police. And what I'd like for you to do is to look at Exhibit 2330, and specifically Article 46 on the law of internal affairs, and I'd like for you to look at it.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Which article, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Article 46, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I've read Article 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. After reading that article, based on your practice in municipalities and your experience as a lawyer, does this article somehow infuse the ARK Crisis Staff with the power to order either the police or the military to take specific steps?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: This article, 46, says that "in the foreseen situations, the minister or an official authorised by the minister can issue orders." However, this does not apply to either the president of the Municipal Assembly or any of the Crisis Staff. It only applies to his assistants and his subordinates. But always those employed by the ministry of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm done with that document if you want to hand it back to the usher, and I'm going to change topics. Before the break, sir, you told us that you worked for a construction company. And during that time at the construction company, you became acquainted with Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you work with him on a large construction project outside of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, in the town of Ersaf in Algeria outside the town of Oran.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you work with him just one year?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You told us that during that one year, you became friends with him; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, we spent every day together, we prepared lunches, dinners, we socialised, we went to the beach, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: After that one year you spent working with him on a daily basis, did you continue your friendship with him?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. But just on separate occasions. We met after we had returned to Yugoslavia from time to time for certain celebrations and other occasions. But we didn't socialise on a daily basis, nor did we go to restaurants and taverns together.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Based on the time you spent with him on a daily basis in the construction company, during those times you socialised with him after that one year, in those times did you ever hear or see Mr. Brdjanin express a discriminatory attitude towards non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No chance. 3.000 Algerians worked together with us, there were workers from Split, Pancevo, Belgrade, of all ethnicities. But never, ever a single incident happened on an ethnic basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: But what about after your return to the former Yugoslavia. Based on your socialising with him during that time period, did you ever see an indication of an incorrect attitude towards non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No, never. On the contrary. Upon his return, a Muslim and he established a company together with his wife, where they worked together. Other Muslims also worked there. And there was no conflict breaking out on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During the years 1991 and 1992, did you know that Mr. Brdjanin was involved in municipal government in the Municipality of Celinac?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was president of the Executive Committee of Celinac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: During his tenure there, was he also an assemblyman on the republic level?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, he was an MP in the National Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was elected in the late 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you aware of his relationship with the Muslim population in his municipality of Celinac?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Well, I know that personally, between him or any other citizen were any conflicts, even on one occasion, I heard, but I didn't witness it personally, that he took part in trying to calm down the situation that broke out between the Serbs and the Muslims, and that he attempted to return the Muslims to the villages that they had abandoned. But that is only what I heard; I didn't witness it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Assuming with me that that was the case, what was the basis for his authority to do something in his home municipality of Celinac? Was it his authority as an MP or something else, if you know?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: He was president of the Executive Committee. And at the same time, he was an MP. He was born there. And he enjoyed considerable authority in his place where he lived, and people respected him so. Accordingly, he was able to influence relationships between people in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now, based on your knowledge of the area around Banja Luka in 1991 and 1992, your knowledge of what was happening in the Krajina during this time period, do you think that his authority would translate to municipalities such as Prijedor? And by my question, I mean this: Do you think that Mr. Brdjanin, based on that authority, could go to Prijedor and stop discriminatory acts, violent acts against the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I don't think he was able to do that. He was not a known figure in politics before the war, whereas on the other hand, Prijedor had a very strong branch office of SDS. They had their own police; they had a military unit. And I don't believe that Brdjanin could actually have an influence in Prijedor, or rather that anyone would listen to him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you think his title as president of the ARK Crisis Staff would have had any effect in Prijedor or a municipality such as Krupa or Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I don't think so. Maybe in Kotor Varos, maybe, because it was closer to Celinac and he knew some people. But as for Prijedor or Krupa, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Now in your testimony just a few minutes ago, you described how Mr. Brdjanin had a very correct attitude towards the Muslims that he worked with, the non-Serbs he worked with. Yet, I know from reading your statements given to the Prosecutor that you're aware of statements that he made that are totally inconsistent with that. My question: Is you're aware of those speeches, those statements made in public. Correct?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Brdjanin, during especially election campaigns, he was capable of saying anything at those public rallies. And he was able, including other SDS members, virtually competing in who would use more abusive language.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Based on the Radoslav Brdjanin that you know, do you think those public statements were the real Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No, no. We who knew him, we would always tell him afterwards, but he would just laugh and say "I didn't do that." When we quoted him, then he would just wave his hand and say "oh, this is just political game." So he had two faces; one was for the public, and it was really inconceivable how this person could have said those things. And he had another face when he was at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did you take him seriously when he made statements such as that?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Well, I just warned him whenever we met, but we didn't meet frequently, that that was not good. That both I and other people who knew him, we would just wave our hands and say, "he's just crazy Brdjo." However, it could incite fear in other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There's one final -- a couple of final areas that I want to go over with you. And I'd like for you to see DB188. And this is a new document that was provided to the Chamber and counsel. I'd like for you to take the chance to read it. I know that I've never showed it to you. But I'd like for you to read it and let me know when you're done with that document. Have you had the chance to look at it and read it?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. The two that were with me, they invited me, and I attended one meeting in the company called Batros Hotel Banja Luka. And when I realised Mr. Jugovic wanted to dismiss a director who was more skilled and professional than he was, I never went to another meeting of this organ or take part in its work. Mr. Jugovic managed to replace the person who was there before him, even though he was less skilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether or not the proportional representation reflected in DB188, that is, workers at more organisations and enterprises would be 70 per cent Serb, 15 per cent Croat, and 15 per cent Muslim, do you know if that was ever -- was that achieved?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I don't know. It's not clear to me whether this has ever been achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm almost done with you, and I appreciate you being concise with your answers. I want to ask you some questions based on your knowledge of Mr. Brdjanin during the time frame 1991, say, through the end of the war. Were you aware of Mr. Brdjanin's attitude towards war profiteers?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Brdjanin was really a single individual who had courage to speak publicly against war profiteers. However, I'm not sure whether he spoke about that during the war or after the war. But I do know that he did speak about that, and I watched him on TV and read about that in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Different topic: Some witnesses have suggested that camps at Keraterm, Omarska were common knowledge to people in Banja Luka. Let me ask you, sir, you were in municipal government. Did you find out about -- when did you find out about these camps?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Just a correction: I was an administrative staff, secretary of the Municipal Assembly. I was not in the government. As for these camps, I learned about them a few days after they had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What do you mean "after they had been established"? Did you find out from someone in government or through the media?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I learned that through the media. Namely, all that happened very swiftly, in a day or two. There were attacks on Kozarac. And I don't know what actually took place there. But the fact is the Muslim population from Kozarac was partly housed in those collection centres or camps as you call them. So a number of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And my last question may have been caused by what I am told is an error in translation. At line 21 of page -- excuse me, line 23 of page 108, the answer is: "As for these camps, I learned about them a few days ago -- a few days after they were established." I'm told by Mr. Vujic that it's published. So I'd like to see if that's clarified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose I can put the question to him. You've understood what the problem is. Perhaps you can clarify this for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After I had found out about these camps through the media, and it was not more than four or five days after that, representatives of the International Red Cross came to Banja Luka and talked with Mr. Radic, mentioning harsh conditions, specifically in Omarska. Therefore, I know, and I heard it both from them and through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's been cleared up. It has also been suggested that a mass killing on Mount Vlasic at a place called Koricanske Stijene was a public secret and all through the Krajina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would prefer that these questions not be prefaced by "there's been a suggestion that", "witnesses have said", anything like that. I think he can just ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In 1992, was it a public secret that there had been a massacre on Mount Vlasic at a location called Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: I didn't know about that. I had not heard of it. If it was a secret, it was a secret. It was not public. I didn't know really and honestly. Truly, I didn't know about that incident. And I know nothing with regard to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Some final questions, and then I'll pass you to Mr. Nicholls. During 1991, 1992, were the conditions such that you knew what was going on in Sipovo?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about Sipovo until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What about Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: Well, Kotor Varos was a very special case. There were massive forces, Muslim forces concentrated there, and there was a place there called Vecici where Serbian policemen were massacred sometime in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there, because you went a little bit too far. And I'm not criticising. Here's my question with respect to Kotor Varos or any other municipality: Would there be any reason for you to be reading Crisis Staff minutes from other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: Branko Cvijic
utterances.text: No, no. We never received those, nor did we know what was taking place. What I'm telling you is what I learned from the media and once I was present personally at the funeral of the people killed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Cunningham. So the agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would prefer it, Your Honour, rather than go for ten minutes and take a break, and I don't think -- I wouldn't finish today. So we would have to be here tomorrow in any event. And I can definitely finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it requires three hours more minus one --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly when I finish, but I would definitely finish by the normal time, I would think, probably before 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be here another day. And we hope to finish with your testimony for sure tomorrow, after which you will be free to go back home. We sat this afternoon to make sure that we would finish with your testimony by tomorrow. You will have an early evening. We are going to break now. And we will adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 I think in this same courtroom. I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
